articles.title: 2 women shot by female colleague at Iowa post office in US; 3 injured, suspect held
articles.summary: A female postal employee allegedly shot two of her female colleagues at the main post office in Des Moines, the capital of Iowa, on Thursday before being
articles.body: A female postal employee allegedly shot two of her female colleagues at the main post office in Des Moines, the capital of Iowa, on Thursday before being arrested nearby. She is facing multiple charges, including attempted murder, according to police.According to news agency AP, the accused, identified as 39-year-old Jennifer Christine Pledger of West Des Moines, allegedly stood over one of the women after shooting her and fired another round before continuing to shoot as she fled the building, police said.A male employee also sustained injuries after falling while attempting to escape the shooting. Authorities said none of the injuries were believed to be life-threatening.Des Moines police Sergeant Paul Parizek said all three victims, including women aged 45 and 53 and a 55-year-old man, were taken to hospital. All were reported to be in stable condition.Pledger faces two counts of attempted murder, two counts of willful injury causing serious injury and a charge of intimidation. Attempts by The Associated Press to contact her possible relatives were unsuccessful. Information about whether she had legal representation was not immediately available.The shooting took place on the second floor of the post office, in an area restricted to employees and inaccessible to the public. Witnesses reported hearing between 10 and 12 gunshots, Parizek said.Police received the first emergency calls at around 9:10 am and reached the scene within three minutes. The suspect was apprehended at approximately 9:21 am along a nearby bicycle path without resistance. Officers recovered a 9 mm handgun at the location where she was detained.The post office is situated just north of downtown Des Moines, opposite one of the city's major hospitals.The US postal inspection service said it was investigating the incident in coordination with local, state and federal law enforcement agencies.Iowa governor Kim Reynolds said she was in touch with the department of public safety following the shooting.“We are monitoring the situation and our prayers are with everyone involved,” she wrote in an online post, while expressing gratitude for the swift response by law enforcement agencies.Following the incident, Des Moines public schools temporarily restricted entry and exit at a nearby elementary school, welcome centre and nutrition centre. The restrictions were lifted after police confirmed that the suspect had been taken into custody.History of shootings at US postal facilitiesPrevious shootings at postal facilities have prompted the US postal service to examine workplace safety and measures to protect employees.In 1986, a disgruntled postal worker carried out a deadly shooting at a post office in Edmond, Oklahoma, killing 14 colleagues before taking his own life.Five years later, in 1991, a former postal employee who had been dismissed from his job shot dead four former colleagues at a post office in Royal Oak, Michigan, before dying by suicide.Following these and other incidents, postal authorities commissioned a study that was released in 2000 to examine workplace violence. The research was conducted around the time the expression “going postal” was gaining popularity in everyday language.The report recommended measures to identify potential warning signs of violent behaviour. However, it also challenged the perception that postal workplaces were particularly prone to violence, concluding that postal employees were less violent than the wider national workforce.Despite the findings, further attacks have occurred at postal facilities.In 2006, a former postal worker stormed a sorting facility in Goleta, California, and fatally shot six employees before taking his own life.You use AI every day. articles.title: 2026 set to be second-hottest year ever recorded; El Nino yet to peak
articles.summary: The planet is heading for another year of extreme heat, with 2026 likely to rank as the second-hottest year ever recorded as an exceptionally strong El
articles.body: The planet is heading for another year of extreme heat, with 2026 likely to rank as the second-hottest year ever recorded as an exceptionally strong El Niño adds to the warming caused by human activities. The warning comes as global temperatures continue to hover above the critical 1.5°C threshold, raising fresh concerns about the pace of climate change.According to the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service, 2026 has a 20 per cent chance of matching or surpassing 2024 as the warmest year on record, while global temperatures are virtually certain to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels this year.The four-year average global temperature from 2023 to 2026 is also expected to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, marking a significant warning for the Paris Agreement's goal of limiting long-term global warming to 1.5°C.October 2026 was the warmest October ever recorded, with global average surface air temperatures reaching 1.75°C above pre-industrial levels (1850-1900), according to Copernicus. It also marked the third consecutive month in which global temperatures exceeded the 1.5°C threshold."October has continued the pattern of remarkable global warmth, with record global and surface ocean temperatures," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which operates Copernicus.She added that an exceptionally strong El Niño was adding further heat to a climate already warmed by human activities.The 1.5°C threshold refers to the global warming limit that countries agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, which aims to restrict the rise in average global temperatures to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels (1850-1900).Scientists warn that exceeding this limit over the long term could significantly intensify extreme weather events, including heatwaves, droughts, floods and rising sea levels.El Niño yet to peak, 2027 could be hotterThe World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has warned that the ongoing El Niño is expected to intensify further and could become one of the strongest events ever recorded.The phenomenon is forecast to peak towards the end of 2026, with its effects likely to persist into early 2027.According to the WMO, the warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean is expected to push sea surface temperatures to exceptional levels, increasing the likelihood of extreme heat and disrupting rainfall patterns across several parts of the world.El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon characterised by the abnormal warming of surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. It occurs every two to seven years and influences weather patterns far beyond the Pacific, increasing the risk of droughts in some regions and heavy rainfall and flooding in others.Its effects vary across countries and seasons, but a particularly strong event can intensify heatwaves and put pressure on agriculture, water supplies and ecosystems.The WMO has warned that the strengthening phenomenon could bring above-average temperatures to much of the world, while shifting rainfall patterns and increasing the risks of droughts and floods.Its warming impact on global temperatures is often felt most strongly in the year following its development, raising concerns that 2027 could surpass previous records to become the hottest year on record.

articles.title: Russell Brand: Met Police boss 'wouldn't be surprised' if more allegations made about disgraced star
articles.summary: Sir Mark Rowley tells the BBC that what he heard reported from Brand's trial came close to "victim blaming".
articles.body:
The head of the Metropolitan Police has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about Russell Brand.

Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".

On Thursday, the entertainer and comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also spoken about the case, seeking to explain the Labour Party's previous association with Brand, saying "it's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life".

Some within the party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.

Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.

In 2014, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted in support of Brand on Twitter following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.

It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.

Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned with.

In his 2014 tweet, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".

Speaking on Friday, Burnham told the BBC: "His crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here.

"All I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do."

Speaking to the BBC on Friday, Sir Mark said that he "wouldn't be surprised if more people came forward" about Brand and said there were "two ongoing rape investigations" into him.

Brand has already been interviewed under caution in relation to those allegations.

In his interview Sir Mark praised the "bravery" of the women who came forward to tell "their story" to the police and during the trial.

"That's a real challenge for anyone having gone through something so ghastly and you have to admire them."

The head of the Met also said that whilst Brand's case "may look different because it's about celebrity, the majority of sex offending is about people abusing power", adding that victims will be believed.

"We will do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful person who is responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life," he said.

It was put to Sir Mark during an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme that Brand's defence barrister "told jurors none of the complainants had in his words 'resisted, screamed or even tried to leave'".

Sir Mark said that what he heard reported from the trial was "very close to victim blaming".

Asked whether he would support the Victim's Commissioner's call for a legal duty in the Courts and Tribunals Bill that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

He said he would "strongly support" that call, adding: "It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case."

Brand was refused bail following his conviction on Thursday and will now spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to the same court on Monday for sentencing.

He is expected to face a substantial prison sentence.

Once the trial was over, it was reported that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation "remains ongoing".

Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.

During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.

During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.

The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

A man who was accused of laughing while Russell Brand sexually assaulted a woman in 2009, has been asked "to step back" from his employer while they consider the verdicts.

Jack Bayles was part of his entourage in 2009 and was said to be present when one of the sexual assaults took place.

Brand had been working on a Channel 4 project when he laid his head into the groin area of a woman who was helping him at the time.

During the trial, the victim told the court Jack Bayles and another member of staff of Brand's had asked her to give the comedian a massage, and said he wouldn't continue unless she did. Shortly after - he sexually assaulted her.

She had complained to her manager - who told the court through a statement at the trial that the victim had described how the men had laughed while the attack took place.

In recent years, Jack Bayles has been working for the TV production company, Various Artists Ltd, as their head of comedy.

In a statement, they told the BBC: "We have asked Jack Bayles to step back from the company whilst we consider the verdict and events surrounding the trial. Our thoughts, though, are primarily with every one of Brand's victims at this time."

According to his biography on the Various Artists Ltd website, Bayles commissioned shows for Channel 4 including two series Derry Girls and Aisling Bea's This Way Up, plus Back, Year Of The Rabbit, Frank Of Ireland and Hullraisers.

In a statement, Mr Bayles said he was sorry but doesn't remember the sexual assault.

"I am appalled and sickened by Brand's actions and have co-operated fully and voluntarily with the investigation and endeavoured to assist as best I can," he said.

"However, I do not remember the incident that took place 17 years ago in 2009. But I acknowledge that I clearly missed something at the time and did not see nor recognise that it caused distress. For that I am sincerely sorry."

He said at the time of the offence he was in the early stages of his career, calling it "a frantic, pressured and toxic working environment".

He described Brand as someone who was "chaotic, dismissive and manipulated the people around him".

The producer said this was why he decided to stop working with him in 2010, adding he "has not had any contact with him since", and that when he worked with him, no complaints were made to him about Brand's behaviour.

"I am unaware if any were raised to anyone else more senior to me," he said.

"I would never willingly or proactively wish to make anyone feel uncomfortable, unsafe or unsupported at work. If I was ever present when Brand acted inappropriately and I failed to spot it and step in, then I sincerely apologise".

articles.title: TikTok risks billions in fines as EU targets its 'rabbit hole' algorithm system
articles.summary: TikTok could face a fine of up to 6 per cent of its global annual turnover after European Union regulators accused the platform of failing to address the
articles.body: TikTok could face a fine of up to 6 per cent of its global annual turnover after European Union regulators accused the platform of failing to address the harmful effects of its recommendation algorithm, which can trap users in a continuous stream of similar videos.The European Commission, the EU's executive arm and digital regulator, issued preliminary findings against TikTok on Friday under the bloc's Digital Services Act (DSA). The action concerns the platform's so-called "rabbit hole" effect, in which its algorithm repeatedly recommends similar content based on what users watch, like or engage with, making it difficult for them to move away from a particular type of content.The Commission said TikTok had failed to introduce reasonable and effective measures to reduce these risks. It warned that repeated exposure to videos dealing with sadness, isolation and body image could negatively affect users' mental health."Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement."Today's preliminary findings show again that TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users' well-being, including those of minors," she said.The Commission has called on TikTok to change the way its 'For You' feed recommends videos. It has suggested giving greater importance to users' explicit preferences, making controls over recommendations easier to find and use, and regularly assessing the impact of its algorithm.The charges come amid growing international concern about the effects of social media on children's mental health. Governments across the world are considering or introducing restrictions on underage users as pressure mounts on technology companies to make their platforms safer.TikTok's Chinese parent company, ByteDance, could face a penalty of up to 6% of its global annual turnover if the company fails to address the concerns raised by the Commission. The preliminary findings are not a final decision, and TikTok will have an opportunity to respond.The action is part of a wider EU investigation into TikTok's compliance with the Digital Services Act, which requires large online platforms to take stronger measures against illegal and harmful content.In February, EU regulators had also issued preliminary findings against TikTok over its allegedly addictive design, inadequate safeguards for children and restrictions that made it difficult for researchers to access public data.TikTok had rejected those findings as "categorically false" and said it would challenge them.The European Commission is also examining similar concerns involving Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram, focusing on whether their recommendation systems create comparable rabbit hole effects.You use AI every day. articles.title: Childminder who left more than 20 children alone in her home jailed
articles.summary: Amanda Mathewson was caught neglecting children at her home in Dunfermline after being spied on by parents.
articles.body:
A childminder who admitted leaving children she was caring for alone and unsupervised in her home has been jailed for two years.

More than 20 unattended children, two under the age of one, were in Amanda Mathewson's house in Dunfermline, Fife, when she was arrested in August 2024.

Her offending only came to light after concerned parents spied on her leaving for a school run without their children.

An internal Care Inspectorate probe found Mathewson, who was been licensed to look after eight children under the age of 16 at any one time, had been tipped off about inspections by an unknown staff member.

Mathewson previously pled guilty to wilfully neglecting, abandoning and exposing children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering or injury to their health.

Sheriff John MacRitchie said Mathewson had committed a "gross abuse of a position of trust" during sentencing at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court.

He read victim impact statements from parents of affected children who described them suffering from "nightmares and anxiety" and developing a "distrust of childcare providers".

Neglect case childminder was 'master manipulator', say parents

Childminder who left 27 children alone in her home pleads guilty to neglect

Mathewson had been a self-employed childminder for 30 years prior to her arrest.

An unannounced visit by the Care Inspectorate in August 2023 rated areas including care, learning and the setting as "very good", praising her "warmth, kindness and nurturing approach".

But a year later, one couple became suspicious that all was not as it seemed.

A friend had mentioned their two children, aged one and three, were not with Mathewson when she was on a school run.

BBC Scotland News has spoken to the father of the children. He has not been named to protect their identity.

The couple watched Mathewson in secret on 26 August 2024, parking opposite her home when their two boys were meant to be in her care as she went to collect other children from a local primary school.

They saw Mathewson leave the home with two young girls in a pushchair, then went to the front door - where the father said a child could be heard "screaming" inside.

The couple walked through a side gate to get to the back garden where they found a number of unsupervised children playing.

They were able to enter the property through the back door, finding a child "lying under a table" crying in severe distress.

Upstairs, the father said "a dozen or so young children" were sitting on the floor of a spare bedroom, with another on a double bed, as a TV on top of a chest of drawers loudly played a children's programme.

He said two others were "tightly strapped into a buggy in a way it was not meant to be used".

"It was August. It was a particularly warm summer. It was hot in that room," he said.

"There was no food, no water, no toys, no activities for the children to be engaged in."

The father said he was cradling two of the children in his arms as he walked downstairs when Mathewson returned home.

He described her reaction to seeing him as being "like her soul had left her body".

"I'll never forget it, she was like a child caught in the act of doing something they shouldn't be doing," he said.

"She took her jacket off and she just slumped to the floor. I asked her; 'Amanda, what the hell? How many laws have you broken here?'"

"It's obvious to us now. Her entire life was a lie. She has fabricated pretty much her entire life, her entire personality. It just crumbled in an instant."

Mathewson was arrested and charged a short time later. When police arrived at the home, she had 15 children aged under 12 in her care, as well as 10 children under primary school age and two children under the age of one.

During the subsequent investigation, various children told their parents that being left alone in Mathewson's home was commonplace.

Parents also raised concerns that their children had not eaten or had anything to drink during her care.

Some also reported their children returning home in dirty nappies.

A court hearing was later told how Mathewson would play loud music and prevented parents from coming into her home in an attempt to hide her offending.

Another parent told BBC Scotland News his daughter was "rummaging in a food waste bin" at nursery after spending mornings at Mathewson's home.

For months after her arrest, he said his daughter would become "distraught" whenever they drove past her house.

He said it became "really difficult" for the family to travel from one side of the town to the other without her becoming distressed.

"I can't imagine what must be going through her mind, the fear of going back there," he said.

"That was heartbreaking and we didn't know what to do or how to help."

He described Mathewson's system of avoiding parents bumping into each other at the same time as being like a "military operation".

"We were let down. We were lied to. Our children were neglected," he said.

The Care Inspectorate's August 2023 visit was meant to be unannounced, but the regulator has since admitted it is likely Mathewson received "confidential information" about inspections from an employee.

The insider is yet to be identified, despite an internal investigation.

A spokesperson for the Care Inspectorate said Mathewson "broke the trust" of families.

They said "inspection, complaints and conflict of interest procedures" had been updated in following feedback from affected parents.

Maria Lloyd, independent chairwoman of the Fife child protection committee, said a "learning review" would take place in the wake of the case.

She said it would consider whether improvements to "practice, processes or partnership working" were required.

A Scottish government spokesperson said the Care Inspectorate had carried out an audit of the way complaints against Mathewson were handled.

They added: "We know Scotland's childminding community will be deeply distressed by this case.

"We are working with the independent regulators to strengthen practice, improve processes and enhance transparency."

Law firm Irwin Mitchell Scotland - who are representing a number of families involved - said they have been instructed to explore a civil case against the Care Inspectorate.

Partner Kim Leslie said: "It is beggars belief that a failing of this magnitude could go unnoticed.

"This is a fundamental breach of trust which, by the regulator's own admission, completely compromised the efficacy of regulatory scrutiny.

"The parents want the Care Inspectorate to be held to account."

articles.title: Born to be torn: A generation raised under Houthi rule in Yemen
articles.summary: As children are recruited to fight, the cost of failing to confront the Houthis is being felt far beyond Yemen.
articles.body:
Nearly eight years ago, I warned about a generation of Yemeni children growing up under Houthi rule. At a time when some were still hoping that people in Saada, northern Yemen, would rise against the group, I questioned what would become of an entire generation raised under its control.

Today, that warning carries a devastating weight. Children born under Houthi rule are now being recruited to fight. Schools and summer camps have been used for indoctrination and military training, exposing young people to recruitment when they should be receiving an education and building a future. These practices were documented by the United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen and the US Department of Labor.

A childhood consumed by fear cannot simply be restored when the guns fall silent. The damage reaches into education, livelihoods, relationships, and the ability to imagine a life beyond war. UNICEF describes the profound effects of disrupted schooling on children’s learning, emotional development, and mental health.

This is why waiting for an uprising against the Houthis has never been a sufficient strategy. People living under coercion face consequences that distant observers do not. Silence under repression cannot be treated as consent, nor can survival be mistaken for allegiance.

But the consequences of allowing Houthi power to grow extend far beyond the people living under its control. The recent attacks across Aden, Hadramout, Shabwa, and Saudi Arabia show how urgently international policy must confront this threat.

In Aden, the October 15 attack on Maashiq Palace brought explosions and renewed fear to the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government. A subsequent reported attack on Aden’s airport on October 21 further underscored the vulnerability of a city whose residents need dependable access to transport and essential services.

For the people of Aden, renewed bombardment carries the memory of earlier battles alongside the anxiety of what comes next. A population struggling to rebuild should not repeatedly be forced to organise daily life around the possibility of another missile.

In Hadramout, reports on October 21 described strikes on Al-Rayyan International Airport in Mukalla, with no injuries initially reported. The AFP news agency also reported that a military base at the airport was hit. The presence of military facilities does not diminish the importance of protecting civilians and the infrastructure on which they depend. Airports connect people to medical treatment, employment, relatives, and the outside world.

In Shabwa, the October 19 missile attack hit the Al-Alam training camp for security forces, causing mass casualties. The Reuters news agency reported dozens killed and more than 200 injured, citing the governor. The strike dealt a devastating blow to personnel responsible for maintaining local security, with losses felt far beyond the camp, in the communities mourning their dead and caring for the wounded.

Across the border, attacks on Saudi airports have killed civilians and disrupted international travel. The October 10 strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people. Travellers of different nationalities have been exposed to a conflict they did not choose. The danger already extends beyond Yemen’s borders.

Together, these attacks reveal the failure of an approach that has not sufficiently constrained Houthi capabilities. Diplomatic activity cannot be measured by meetings held or assurances received while missiles continue to reach cities, airports, and vital infrastructure.

The record also demands clarity about the Houthis’ terrorist designations. Yemen’s National Defence Council designated the group a terrorist organisation in October 2022, and the United States designated it a Foreign Terrorist Organization, effective March 5, 2025. In my judgement, their documented conduct amply warrants those decisions.

Other governments should take those designations and the evidence behind them seriously. Engagement must carry conditions, verification, and consequences. The Houthis signed a UN action plan in April 2022 to end grave violations against children, including recruitment. Subsequent reporting by Human Rights Watch documented continued child recruitment. Commitments must therefore be judged by their implementation, not merely by the signing of documents.

Token penalties or political rewards for terrorism would set a dangerous precedent in international relations: Violence wins concessions, and armed coercion buys political power. Other armed groups could draw the same lesson, potentially including groups closer to home for the countries failing to act.

A credible response must disrupt illicit weapons supplies and financing, strengthen civilian protection, defend maritime navigation, and impose targeted consequences on those directing and enabling abuses. Humanitarian assistance and legitimate commerce must remain protected. Civilians should never pay twice: First for Houthi repression, then for measures intended to confront it.

Protecting the next generation also requires sustained investment in education, independent information, psychosocial care, and the reintegration of children released from armed groups. UNICEF’s child protection work in Yemen includes psychosocial support and reintegration assistance. Preventing recruitment means giving children and their communities a viable future.

North and South Yemen face immediate dangers, and Saudi Arabia and international shipping have already felt the consequences. No government should assume that a threat left to grow will remain geographically contained.

Nearly eight years after my warning, another generation cannot be asked to wait. The threat is established. International policy must finally match it.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Train worker recalls repelling Huntingdon attacker with frying pan
articles.summary: Samir Zitouni used a frying pan against train attacker Anthony Williams, jurors hear.
articles.body:
A train staff member who used a frying pan against a man accused of trying to kill 10 people on board said he did not want to "give up until the train stopped", a court has heard.

Samir Zitouni was working on the York to London King's Cross LNER service on 1 November last year when Anthony Williams attacked, leading to an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire.

Cambridge Crown Court heard Zitouni said he was trying to hit the knife Williams was holding and "not let him pass".

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 10 counts of attempted murder, and four other alleged attempted murders in earlier incidents in Peterborough and London.

Jurors were played a video interview with Zitouni, who watched on from the public gallery.

The court has previously heard about the injuries suffered by Zitouni during the attack.

Both his lungs were punctured and he needed four blood transfusions, chest drains and the assistance of a ventilator.

In his video interview, Zitouni said he saw a crowd of people come through the train shouting "there's a guy with a knife", to which he said "a guy with a knife, are you sure?".

Jurors have heard from another injured passenger, Raza Aslam, that Zitouni "was rushing backwards and forwards like a busy beaver trying to get different things" including trolleys and pans to defend the passengers.

Zitouni said he had taken the pan, then "the first thing I saw was the blade of the knife".

He said he was saying: "No, man. No, man". Zitouni asked the attacker to stop, offering help, and saying he thought that "was better than swearing at him".

He said: "I was terrorised, it was hard to believe."

Jurors have been shown CCTV footage from the train, and previously heard Zitouni was said to have told the defendant: "We love you, we can help you."

In his video interview, he said: "My thinking was try to hit the knife, to drop his knife... to not let him pass, to not give up until the train stopped."

He said he told a colleague: "I think I'm going to die."

Passenger Michael Gawthorpe, who was not stabbed by Williams but was in the same carriage as Zitouni, said in a video-recorded interview that he "kept saying calm down, just put the knife down, please stop... we've all got kids".

He said Williams said something along the lines of "they're trying to kill me".

He recalled someone had passed him a large toaster, so he threw it at the attacker, jurors heard.

But he said he remembered Williams then looking at him and he thought "that was pretty much it for me at this point".

"I was pretty scared. I thought that was me done," Gawthorpe said.

However, the train began to slow down and he said this "may have distracted him".

Another passenger, Christina Jones, wept in a video-recorded interview played to the jury as she demonstrated how she hid behind her handbag.

The court heard she threw a hot drink at Williams.

As well as arguing Williams was attempting to murder the 10 people on the train, prosecutors allege that on 31 October he tried to kill three people in Peterborough.

He is also charged with attempting to murder a teenager in the early hours of 1 November on a DLR train in east London.

Whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question - the court has been told - but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill.

articles.title: Six arrests over Meadow Well Bonfire Night violence
articles.summary: Police believe the disorder in Meadow Well relates to misinformation over the future of a building.
articles.body:
Six people, including three teenage boys, have been arrested after a night of violence saw fireworks and bricks launched at emergency services on Bonfire Night.

Northumbria Police said its crews had been attacked after responding to reports of anti-social behaviour in the Waterville Road area of Meadow Well in North Tyneside at about 21:00 GMT on Thursday.

A number of officers were injured and five police cars and three fire engines were damaged during the disorder, which was linked to misinformation that the building would be a house of multiple occupation (HMO) for asylum seekers, the force said.

Ch Supt Daniel Whyte said anyone involved in the disorder should expect a "knock on the door".

Two men, aged 25 and 27, a 27-year-old woman, and three teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of violent disorder and remain in custody.

Whyte said there would be an increased police presence in the area to "offer reassurance".

Ian Miller, who runs the local community centre The Meadows, said people had a right to feel safe where they live.

He told BBC Radio Newcastle emergency services should not have had to experience assaults and "rioting and causing this amount of trouble gets you nowhere".

He said those who had been engaged in the violence did not represent most people living in the area.

Miller said his team had been aware of rumours circulating about the building for the past few weeks.

To counter them, the community centre held a meeting for residents last month alongside the building's developer, who had emphasised the site was due to be turned into a supermarket.

The flats above would be occupied by anyone who went through the "process of getting somewhere to live", including people from the estate, he said.

The police confirmed the flats above the supermarket would be for private rental.

Miller said people in the area were "creative, positive, enthusiastic, wonderful folk" and not reflected in what had happened.

"Those people exist here, live here and they have a right to enjoy and feel safe where they live," he said.

Litter picker Dave Shaw, 76, said about 60 youths had been throwing missiles at firefighters.

He saw five or six young people letting off fireworks towards the building and then black smoke, so he knew it had caught fire, he said.

"There were about 60 of them, throwing bricks and whatever else they could find at the police," he said.

Shaw initially believed a petrol bomb had also been thrown but he later realised it was a smoke grenade.

North East Mayor Kim McGuinness said she was "disgusted" by the violence which she said was carried out by a "minority of idiots".

North Tyneside mayor Karen Clark said the disorder was appalling and completely unacceptable.

"I know how much pride the people of Meadow Well take in their community and how upsetting and frightening these scenes will have been for residents," she said.

Clark also condemned a post made at the scene by Reform UK councillor Steven Robinson who represents the Chirton and Percy Main ward.

Robinson's post, seen by the Local Democracy Reporting Service , mentioned asylum accommodation and said residents should be told if "if the government wants to use buildings in our community for that purpose".

Clark said Reform politicians should be correcting misinformation and "spreading it has real consequences for our communities".

North Shields Green councillor Martin Osborne said the planning application was "clear" about what the building was going to be and Robinson had chosen to "stoke division in our communities with an ambiguous post".

Robinson said he condemned the violence and, when he arrived, "order had been restored" and he "did what I could to help keep things calm".

articles.title: 1Xtra launches first ever UK rap chart for 'fair playing field'
articles.summary: The top 20 best selling UK rap tracks will be celebrated each week on Radio 1Xtra with DJ Kenny Allstar.
articles.body:
British rap artists will step into the spotlight later when BBC Radio 1Xtra launches the first ever dedicated rap chart based on UK listening figures.

DJ Kenny Allstar, who'll host the countdown on Friday nights, has one word: "Finally".

"If we have our own fair playing field where we can all be celebrated... it then feels fair and it feels exciting," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

Currently artists compete across genres for a spot in the Official Singles Chart, but Allstar says this is dominated by pop music, making it harder for other genres to be heard.

Perhaps with the exception of heavyweights like Central Cee and Dave, who broke chart records with Sprinter back in 2023 , "it's not easy for any artist to go against Sabrina Carpenter and Taylor Swift every week," he says.

Compiled by the Official Charts Company, 20 rap singles from British artists will be ranked each week based on streams and sales in the UK.

It follows the launch of other genre-specific charts including for R&B, 'homegrown' albums and British Asian music.

Allstar hopes it'll give UK rap a boost as he acknowledges it has taken a bit of a beating recently with prominent artists like Skepta and Digga saying the quality of music coming from the scene has dipped.

"Future broadcasters and talent will benefit from this forever, I'm super gassed."

Allstar has long been a champion of UK rap and currently presents the Rap Show on BBC Radio 1, which he describes as "the show I always wanted as a kid".

This new role is "a pinch me moment," he says.

The Official Charts Company previously listed the 40 top selling R&B and hip hop tracks on its website, but there had been nowhere for fans to listen to the chart.

"It was literally just a bunch of numbers and text, so it kind of existed but not in this capacity," Allstar says.

Each week will likely see at least three or four new artists in the chart, giving emerging talent a chance to be heard by hundreds of thousands of listeners.

"What we can finally have is UK rap having its dedicated space where artists can just be celebrated," he says.

Eric Hunter, from the Official Charts Company, says the countdown will be "an amazing opportunity to shine a light on more artists, document the culture and give emerging talent a way to track their progress alongside their peers".

The company says UK rap is "one of the country's most influential and fast-moving music scenes" and the chart will celebrate both established names and the next generation of rappers driving the scene.

The debut show coincides with Skepta's long-awaited sixth studio album and Allstar says he expects to see the rapper feature in the chart.

"It's looking promising, but the only way you can find out is if you listen in," he says.

The Official UK Rap Chart will broadcast on 1Xtra each Friday from 22:00-23:00 and will be available after on BBC Sounds.

articles.title: Turtle to return to sea after 22 years at Irish aquarium
articles.summary: After two decades in the care of Dingle Oceanworld Aquarium the turtle rescued in 2004 is finally well enough to return to the wild.
articles.body:
Mary Cronin's children Barry and Aisling were still young when the family found a severely injured sea turtle buried beneath storm debris on an Irish beach.

More than 22 years later, Barry and Aisling have grown up and moved abroad and now Molly the loggerhead has left Ireland too.

After two decades of gradual rehabilitation and veterinary care advances, the rescued turtle has been released back into the ocean.

Because of severe injuries to her front flippers, believed to have been caused by a shark attack, staff feared she might never be strong enough to survive at sea.

Molly was rescued by Dingle Oceanworld Aquarium in 2004 and was there until May 2026 when she moved to to Zoomarine Porto d'Abrigo centre in Portugal.

She was released about 12 nautical miles off the Algarve coastline on Wednesday 28 October.

"We couldn't be any prouder of her. Getting turtles back to the ocean is always our goal, and this is just the start of a new chapter for Molly," Oceanworld Aquarium said in a social media post.

Molly is also carrying a satellite tag so the team at Zoomarine can track her.

Mary, from Wexford, said she and her children found the turtle while walking on a beach near Castlegregory on the Dingle peninsula in County Kerry after an Atlantic storm.

"The beach was full of seaweed and debris," she told BBC News NI.

"Something moved in the seaweed and there was this turtle."

Molly was "cold-stunned" - a form of hypothermia that affects sea turtles in cold waters.

The family called the aquarium whose team arrived within half an hour with heated water tanks.

Mary named the turtle Molly after her own nickname and the family returned to visit the turtle at the aquarium over the years.

"As the children got older, it wasn't every year, but we always called in," Mary said.

"She followed us through life in a very positive way."

Now both Barry and Aisling are living in New Zealand, with Barry working as a conservation biologist and Aisling as a teacher - the imprint Molly left on their lives never went away.

And because of this Mary said Molly's departure feels familiar.

"It's kind of like your child getting on an airplane and going across to another continent," she said.

"We are thrilled that Molly has returned to her native home and looking forward to reports back on her progress out in the wild."

Dr Kevin Flannery, the aquariums director and founder, said previous efforts to fit Molly with prosthetic flippers were unsuccessful.

During a recent medical check-up, staff discovered she was carrying eggs.

"It's important that these creatures get back into the wild and they survive and thrive into the future," he told BBC News NI in June, after she left the aquarium.

Loggerhead turtles have a long life span and can live from 50 to 80 years - or older. They begin laying eggs between 25 and 35.

Flannery said he believes Molly was about 10 years old when she was rescued.

She was taken off display for six months and trained to forage and survive independently.

The aquarium worked with Zoomarine, which has a specialist turtle rehabilitation centre, to prepare her for the transfer and release into the warm Atlantic waters.

DNA testing showed Molly is linked to loggerhead turtles from the Gulf of Mexico and it is hoped she can make her way back there.

Loggerhead turtles are considered vulnerable, meaning they face a high risk of extinction.

Molly may face dangers on her journey back across the open Atlantic including plastic pollution, fishing gear, hooks and boat strikes.

Flannery said Ireland would typically see one or two loggerheads washed ashore each year, although five stranded last year alone.

He said warming seas linked to climate change could lead to more strandings meaning rescue centres must be prepared.

Molly weighed about 12kg (1st 9lb) when rescued and now weighs 120kg (18st 9lb).

"We could have her playing full forward for our All-Ireland teams," he said.

"She's been part and parcel of the aquarium. All the staff got to know her and all the previous staff we've had here down through the 20 odd years.

"But these poor creatures are under threat, so it's vital that Molly gets back to breed."

articles.title: Katherine Ryan says she feels 'grief and relief' after Russell Brand conviction
articles.summary: The comedian had previously spoken about an unnamed "predator" in the entertainment industry.
articles.body:
Comedian Katherine Ryan has said she feels "grief and relief" after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault.

The Canadian stand-up and TV star said there were "a lot of women speaking privately and quietly" following Thursday's verdict, who feel "a very nuanced mix of emotions".

Ryan had previously claimed in a BBC TV documentary interview with Louis Theroux that there was a "predator" in the entertainment industry.

Ryan said in 2022 that she could not name the famous man as it would be a "litigious minefield" but mentioned that she had appeared on a TV programme with him and told him he was a "predator" to "his face".

It was widely rumoured Ryan had been referring to her time on Comedy Central's Roast Battle in 2018 alongside Brand, but she has not confirmed she was referring to him, and she did not name the show she was working on.

Speaking about the guilty verdict of his trial, on the latest episode of her podcast Telling Everybody Everything, Ryan said: "It really made me feel just quite dysregulated again, caught off-guard, emotional, in awe of the survivors who also had nothing to gain.

"They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money, and a legion of fans ready to attack them."

She added: "I will never be someone who like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There's a level of relief, but there's grief alongside relief.

"Everything's nuanced, and it was proved in court that a terrible thing happened, and that means that a terrible thing happened.

"I just think again and again about people who have been hurt, and who have to carry that, who've carried that around long enough, and will continue to carry that in some way, regardless of what justice is done."

Brand was found guilty on Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

The former entertainer was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told him to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

Ryan continued on the podcast: "This verdict came because women were hurt, and I worry as well about what happens next.

"Because he's obviously spent a long time cultivating this idea that the establishment have invented these claims against him, and he's martyred himself to a growing audience who really still think that it is the courageous survivors who are the villains in this story."

Bear Grylls, the adventurer and host of the Discovery Channel's show Man Vs Wild, has spoken about when he helped baptise Brand in the River Thames in 2024.

"Brand's faith seemed genuine to me at the time when I was a guest at his private baptism," he said on X, adding he had attended a few, including "visiting in prisons with people who have committed terrible crimes".

He said he attended as part of a calling of his faith "to love and serve anyone", adding it is "the sick who need healing".

"Judgement is for the courts and God… I wouldn't want to ever discourage someone's coming to faith," he added. "It is right that justice has now been served.

"I can't imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day."

Brand is now also being investigated over further rape allegations made by two women, police have now said.

Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.

Brand was accused by four women of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint Channel 4 Dispatches, Times and Sunday Times investigation in September 2023.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.

On Thursday it emerged that Brand was facing further rape allegations made by two women. The Metropolitan police said he had previously been interviewed under caution in relation to them.

During a pre-trial hearing in October Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer couldn't receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.

Prosecutors opposed Brand's application to have his case stopped.

It was during that hearing that the prosecution said one of the complaints made in the documentary was being investigated.

Riel Karmy-Jones KC said: "Of the four women in the Ch4 documentary, two concern events outside the jurisdiction.

"One did not disclose any offence. The other is being investigated.

"There had been some interaction in 2018, she did not report the matter until 2024, after the documentary was aired."

In documents submitted to the court for the hearing prosecutors also said it was "plainly incorrect" to say there had been a decision not to investigate.

"The outstanding charges against RB in respect of 'Alice' from Dispatches demonstrate that there has been no such decision – rather that the police will and have responded appropriately once a formal allegation is made."

The head of the Metropolitan Police has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about Russell Brand.

Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".

articles.title: Uganda tree-planting scheme loses Welsh government funding
articles.summary: The Welsh government has given more than £4m to the scheme since 2015, but will end it due to budget pressures.
articles.body:
The Welsh government will end funding for a tree-planting scheme in Uganda that was branded "woke" by opposition politicians.

Wales has given more than £4m to climate change charity Size of Wales since 2015, including £350,000 for the current financial year, to work with Indigenous communities to promote tree-planting in the African nation.

Ministers said budgetary pressures meant "difficult decisions" had to be made and the charity would lose its grant for the scheme at the end of March 2027.

Right-wing parties in the Senedd welcomed the decision, and left-wing ones criticised it, with the Welsh Liberal Democrats accusing the Plaid Cymru-run government of "out-Reforming Reform".

Size of Wales works with Indigenous and local people worldwide to grow trees and protect at least two million hectares of tropical forests - an area the size of Wales.

Previous Welsh governments under Labour had started funding its work, which included the tree-planting scheme around Mbale in the Mount Elgon region of eastern Uganda, with 25 million trees planted as of 2025.

Previous criticism by opponents of using taxpayers' money for the scheme led to Labour ministers last year pointing out that it amounted to about £270,000 a year - equivalent to 0.001% of the government's total annual budget in 2025.

A document published in August 2025 by the previous government stated Wales was "helping some of the very poorest people in the world adapt to climate change and improve their livelihoods" and protected local people in the Mount Elgon region from deadly landslides.

Plaid took over the Welsh government in May , with the decision to end the tree-planting scheme coming as it prepares to publish its draft budget for 2026-27 later this month.

A Welsh government spokesperson said it was developing "a new international strategy for Wales" and was "working to ensure that future investment demonstrates impact and value for money and delivers clear benefits for Wales as well as our international partners".

"We do not intend to renew grant funding for the Size of Wales Mbale tree-planting programme beyond its current end date of 31 March 2027," they said.

"That is not a judgement on the quality of the work. The programme has planted millions of trees and built important links between Wales and Uganda, and we look forward to continuing our dialogue with Size of Wales."

The spokesperson said that recognising the success of a programme "is not the same as committing to fund the same delivery model indefinitely", and the government had to "make difficult choices about where limited resources can have the greatest impact".

They added: "We will never retreat from Wales being an outward-looking and globally responsible nation."

The tree-planting scheme has long been criticised by Reform UK and Welsh Conservative politicians in the Senedd.

Reform UK's leader in Wales, Helen Jenner, welcomed the announcement and said her party had been calling "for an end to this ridiculous woke spending for years now".

"We have changed the conversation in Cardiff Bay and demanded that Welsh taxpayers' money be spent in Wales and not sent abroad for things like Ugandan trees," she said.

"Now, thanks to us, Welsh households will not be funding those trees."

The leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd Darren Millar said the decision was "long overdue but it is better late than never".

"It's outrageous that the Welsh government has been spending so much taxpayers' money on planting trees in Africa while our schools and hospitals have not been getting the cash they need," he said.

"It has no responsibility for foreign affairs or international development, so every pound spent on these things is a pound that is being taken away from our NHS, our education system and helping the Welsh economy.

"The Welsh government should put the people of Wales first, not vanity projects overseas."

But the leader of the Welsh Liberal Democrats Jane Dodds described it as a "short-sighted" decision.

"Tackling climate change and protecting nature isn't a luxury," she said.

"Size of Wales has planted millions of trees, built real links between Wales and Uganda, and helped communities protect forests that matter to all of us.

"Plaid are out-Reforming Reform by cutting international funding for work ministers admit has been a success.

"Wales' global responsibility shouldn't be the first thing to go."

Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates said: "In opposition, Plaid Cymru repeatedly championed international programmes.

"Yet again, it seems that what Plaid say is very different to what they actually do."

The Welsh government also provides a grant of £280,000 a year to the charity to deliver an education programme in Welsh schools, which runs until the end of March 2027, with a proposal for the future of the programme to be submitted and considered by the country's rural resilience and sustainability minister.

articles.title: King Charles emerges as UK's diplomatic 'secret weapon' amid challenging international relations
articles.summary: King Charles is increasingly being called upon by the British government to handle sensitive diplomatic engagements, with a senior royal aide describing
articles.body: King Charles is increasingly being called upon by the British government to handle sensitive diplomatic engagements, with a senior royal aide describing the monarch as a "secret weapon" capable of reaching political ground that elected leaders may struggle to navigate.The remarks followed the king's recent Caribbean tour, which included a meeting of the Commonwealth of Nations, where discussions over Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade dominated proceedings. Several leaders called for an apology and reparations, putting the monarch in a difficult diplomatic position.Charles did not issue an apology or commit Britain to reparations, in keeping with government policy. However, his expression of personal sorrow over the suffering caused by slavery was welcomed by several Commonwealth leaders, who viewed it as a step towards addressing the issue.Speaking to reporters after the tour, a senior royal aide described the engagement as complex but said the king had handled it through what he called "statecraft both by word and deed," according to Reuters."It's a great secret weapon to send the king," the aide said, speaking anonymously. He added that Charles could connect with audiences and governments in ways that politicians might find difficult.The comments reflect a growing role for the monarchy in Britain's diplomatic efforts as the government seeks to maintain relationships with international partners. Although the king serves as the country's constitutional head of state and is required to remain politically neutral, successive governments have increasingly used royal engagements to support foreign policy objectives.Charles has also been involved in efforts to maintain Britain's relationship with the United States amid tensions with President Donald Trump, particularly over the Iran war. The monarch hosted Trump during a state visit to Britain and later travelled to the US on a reciprocal visit."We're just in the fifth year of the reign and I think what we're seeing is a very clear pattern emerging of the government asking the king to head into quite politically charged situations, quite challenging situations," the aide said.The aide added that Charles enjoyed working on difficult diplomatic assignments, particularly when they involved repairing relationships with countries where political disagreements had complicated ties."Refreshing and reinvigorating relationships with nations where there have been some complex political issues at play, that is what he lives and breathes for," the aide said.The Caribbean visit comes during another difficult period for the royal family. A recent biography of Charles' first wife, Princess Diana, written by her brother, Charles Spencer, included criticism of the king's response to her death.His younger brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, has also continued to attract negative attention while remaining under police investigation. Andrew has denied wrongdoing. Meanwhile, the return to Britain of Charles' younger son, Prince Harry, has brought further complications for the family.Charles remains head of the Commonwealth and is monarch of 15 countries, including Canada and Australia. However, the future of the monarchy in those nations remains a matter for their governments and citizens. Barbados became the latest country to remove the British monarch as its head of state in 2021.The royal aide said the decision on whether to retain the monarchy rested with individual countries and the Commonwealth."The (royal) family serves when it's wanted and if not, then a new arrangement can be found," the aide said.Charles, who turns 78 this month, is continuing his recovery from cancer. Questions about his health and age have accompanied his recent public engagements, but the aide pointed to the king's activity during the Caribbean tour as evidence of his commitment to the role.In the Bahamas, Charles danced down a street while waving cowbells in temperatures reaching 40 degrees Celsius. He also maintained his sense of humour after being caught in a tropical downpour without an umbrella."This is literally what he was born to do. He's very good at it, and he enjoys the reaction he gets from people," the aide said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: Americans who are planning trips to Europe are being warned about scam websites charging travelers for ETIAS travel authorizations that are not yet available. The European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS) is currently not operating and applications are not being accepted, according to guidance from the European Union. The EU said it will announce the specific launch date several months before the program begins. TRAVELERS MAY FACE MAJOR DISRUPTIONS AS STRIKES THREATEN AIRPORTS AND POPULAR ATTRACTIONS Even so, more than 150 third-party websites have reportedly appeared offering ETIAS-related information or services, as reported by The Guardian. Bobby Laurie, a Pennsylvania-based travel expert and former flight attendant, told Fox News Digital that some sites are designed to appear legitimate when travelers search online for information about European entry requirements. "These scam websites are set up to look like official government websites," Laurie said. The biggest warning sign for travelers right now is the request that they pay for an ETIAS authorization, Laurie said. The EU has also warned travelers about possible abuse by commercial intermediaries, including websites that may make themselves appear to be the official application channel. Other concerns include excessive fees and the possible misuse of personal or financial information, according to the EU. Once ETIAS launches, legitimate third parties will be allowed to submit applications on behalf of travelers. Laurie noted that travelers will also be able to apply themselves through the official EU website. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES For Americans traveling before the ETIAS program takes effect, Laurie recommended checking the official entry requirements for each country on their itinerary, particularly when connecting through countries with separate rules. Travelers who have already provided payment information to a suspicious website should contact their credit card company, Laurie said. He also recommended monitoring for fraudulent charges and considering identity monitoring if passport or other sensitive personal information was provided. "You don't know where that information is going to end up," Laurie said. "They're just banking on you not reading and trying to do something in a hurry," he said. articles.title: Around 1941, Canadian gunner Alfred Sutton recorded a voice message for his wife and sons on aluminium discs; decades later, renovators found them hidden inside the family home’s wall
articles.summary: Discover the fascinating story of Alfred Sutton, a Canadian soldier's voice recordings found hidden in a wall, revealing heartfelt messages to his wife and sons during WWII.
articles.body: A kitchen renovation in the late 1990s exposed a sealed envelope behind a wall, hiding two aluminium discs. The discovery then waited on a machine that could play the recording. The message recorded on two aluminium discs overseas remained sequestered for decades inside a house in Napanee, Ontario. The recordings belonged to a Canadian soldier, Alfred Richard Thomas Sutton, who served with the Royal Canadian Artillery.According to the Lennox and Addington County Museum and Archives, the two records were received as a donation after a couple brought them in for examination. They had discovered the discs in the late 1990s while renovating their kitchen. Inside a sealed envelope behind the wall were the recordings and several wooden gramophone needles. The couple kept the material for more than 20 years before a friend found a player that could play it.Heather Wilson, the museum’s archivist, recorded the discovery in an account published on 6 November 2024. The records turned out to be wartime voice letters, a method used by soldiers to send recorded messages to relatives at home. Sutton’s recordings were addressed to his wife, Constance, and their sons in Strathcona, Ontario.A voice preserved from the Second World WarThe recordings remained unplayed until early 2024, when a friend of the couple found a record player. After that, they took the two discs to Lennox and Addington County Museum and Archives, where the recordings were played for the first time. The first disc was difficult to discern because of the poor audio. The second disc, however, contained a clearer message. It started with Sutton greeting his wife: “Hello, sweetheart… This is Saturday afternoon, September the 27th.” This allowed the archivist to identify its intended recipient and establish an approximate recording date. On the disc, he asked about her and the children, mentioned receiving a parcel and sent his affection to the family. He also spoke about returning to Canada.The disc did not reveal the year when it was recorded. Wilson used the details in the message and the available historical information to place it in 1941. Based on the historical information, Sutton was stationed in Aldershot, England, when he made the recording. By Wilson’s understanding, this likely explains why very few voice letters survived. Her research had documented similar references to such recordings in the United States and the United Kingdom, alongside a small number of Canadian mentions. The museum had no other example in its collection.Sutton’s military service and familyAccording to the Lennox and Addington County Museum and Archives, Sutton was born in Leeds, England, in 1906. He moved to Canada with his family in 1913 and worked as a labourer in Strathcona by the age of 15. Later, he found employment at the local paper mill.In 1939, he married Constance Pringle, and together they had two sons. Subsequently, Sutton enlisted for military service and joined the 14th Field Regiment before being sent to England. Based on his recordings, a brief account of his life overseas was revealed.In the end, Sutton survived the war and returned to Canada. He and Constance lived in the same house where the records were later discovered. By the time of his death, their sons had moved away, one to Saskatoon and the other to Colorado.Sutton died at Lennox and Addington County General Hospital on 12 June 1967, at the age of 61. The circumstances in which the two discs came to be concealed in the first place remained unknown. The couple who found them eventually donated the recordings to the county archives, where they could be played and preserved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A 1945 nuclear test in New Mexico sent fallout to 46 states within 10 days, a new reconstruction finds; Washington and Oregon showed no deposition in the model
articles.summary: A new reconstruction study shows the fallout from the Trinity nuclear test in 1945 spread to 46 US states within 10 days, with significant implications for public health and historical understanding of nuclear weapon impacts.
articles.body: Fallout from the Trinity test, the first nuclear detonation, reached 46 US states within 10 days, a new reconstruction in Scientific Reports finds. According to the Scientific Reports study, the device detonated at 5:29 AM local time on July 16, 1945, atop a tower about 30 m (roughly 100 feet) tall in New Mexico. Only Washington and Oregon showed no deposition in the model. The authors reconstructed the first 10 days of fission-product deposition for 94 of the 101 tests, using publicly available US Government test data, particle-size distribution benchmarked against National Cancer Institute iodine-31 estimates for 51 Nevada tests and NOAA’s HYSPLIT transport model driven by ERA5 weather analysis. It also says Trinity fallout alone reached 46 states within 10 days and an ensemble analysis was used to bound meteorological uncertainty despite its 1945 observations.The study, Reconstruction of fallout deposition from U.S. atmospheric nuclear tests conducted in New Mexico and Nevada, led by Sébastien Philippe, was published in Scientific Reports on August 24, 2026. His group had developed a model for the first 10 days of fission product deposition during 94 of 101 atmospheric tests conducted by the United States from 1945 through 1962. The Trinity test was the first one, while the other hundred tests occurred at the Nevada Test Site. Out of those hundred tests, seven were not associated with any fission product yield.The plume went Northeast first, then spread across the central USThe plume initially travelled northeast from the test site, depositing material across parts of New Mexico, the Midwest and the Great Lakes region. In 48 hours, the fallout spread to the Central part of the United States; also, there was some fallout even further south and west from ground zero. The maximum value of deposition at the Trinity site was 4×10^11 becquerels/m2. The yield of the test was 24.8 kilotons, up from the previous estimate of 21 kilotons, an increase of about 18%.A 1945 weather record and two years of CPU timeOlder Trinity simulations have used limited surface measures and low-resolution weather data, generating only short-range maps. The authors combined NOAA’s HYSPLIT transport model with the ERA5 weather analysis dataset, which was extended back to 1940 in 2023. For July 1945, ERA5 drew on about 2 million observations, split roughly evenly between surface and upper air measurements. To test how much the weather data affected the result, the authors ran the Trinity model with all 10 ERA5 and ensemble members. Deposition reached 46 states in six of the runs and 45 states in the other four. The authors ran HYSPLIT 104 times, once for each of the 94 tests plus 10 ensemble runs for Trinity, with 9 million particles per run. They put the total at about two years of CPU time, spread across 128 threads.Film packaging from Indiana and Iowa offers a check from 1945The reconstruction is consistent with the merge evidence available. The author's evidence of radioactive contamination discovered on strawboard used to package X-ray film from Indiana and Iowa during 1945 is one of the earliest known instances where it was found that fallout from the Trinity test reached great distances. It is also consistent with the 1987 NOAA study of fallout in the first 24 hours.According to the authors, the total deposited activity combined radionuclides that decay at different rates, so it could not be read directly as a measure of risk and converting the maps into doses would require additional modelling. The authors also said the model stopped at the US borders, although the plumes from several tests plausibly extended into Canada and Mexico.The National Cancer Institute modeled New Mexico doses separatelyThat dose work has been done for New Mexico alone. A 2021 technical note in Nuclear Technology, Estimated Radiation to Radioactive Fallout from the Trinity Nuclear Test, summarised the first dose, reconstruction and cancer risk projection for the state's population, which investigators from the National Cancer Institute published in 2020 after working for seven years. The Institute looked at Trinity fallout and cancer risk in New Mexico, whereas the new model covers the whole contiguous United States.A 2016 notice in the Federal Register laid out the plan. The goal of the institute was to calculate doses to the thyroid, stomach and red bone marrow and the population of each county in New Mexico, depending on age, gender and race. The plan included focus groups for people aged 70 and older who were alive at the time of the test. According to the National Cancer Institute’s assessment of the Trinity Test fallout, the highest radiation doses were estimated to have occurred in Torrance and Guadalupe counties. The researchers also projected that several hundred excess cancer cases may have resulted from the exposure, although the exact number remains uncertain.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Meghan Markle's father was taken into custody near Tampa, Fla., the Associated Press reported.
articles.body:
Meghan Markle's father, Thomas Markle, has been arrested in the U.S. on charges related to child sexual abuse material, according to the Associated Press.

Markle, 82, was reportedly arrested at a care home near Tampa, Fla., Friday and was taken away by federal agents. AP said its sources were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.

Last month, it was reported that Markle was under investigation in the Philippines over allegations that he possessed child sexual abuse material. He has not been charged.

The Sun first reported that his son, and Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr., told Philippine police that after his father left the country in May, he discovered images of child sexual abuse material among boxes at his father's former home in Cebu.

Markle Sr. denied those allegations, telling the British newspaper the Daily Mail on Oct. 23: "It's just a bunch of lies. It's sick." He said the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico in January 2025 and that he did not know who had access to them. He said he would welcome a forensic examination of the devices.

Meghan Markle released a statement following the claims, saying she was "deeply distressed." She also revealed she had received a copy of a letter containing "troubling" allegations about him in 2019, which had been sent to London's Metropolitan Police.

"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said. British police subsequently said it had not shared the letter with other law enforcement agencies.

According to British tabloid the Sun on Sunday , Meghan was advised that speaking publicly could jeopardize any potential legal case.

Addressing her decision to keep Archie and Lilibet away from their grandfather over the past few years, Meghan said that "any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them."

She added: "My sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."

Meghan reportedly wrote to her estranged father in December 2025 to tell him she was aware of child abuse allegations against him and would not allow him to meet his grandchildren. Meghan reportedly told her father the letter would be the last time he heard from her.
